title: Temporary Works: The Structures That Hold the Building Up Before It Can Hold Itself
summary: Temporary works such as excavation support, formwork, falsework and back-propping are real structures carrying large and uncertain loads, and they fail more often than permanent buildings. They sit between the permanent engineer and the contractor's methods, so unless the contract assigns them, nobody owns the whole picture.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the most dangerous structures on your site are the ones that will not exist when the building is finished. Temporary works carry heavy, uncertain loads on tight schedules, and the two moments that decide their safety are the permission to load and the permission to strike.

In plain English

Temporary works are everything built to make the permanent works possible and later removed: excavation support and dewatering, formwork that moulds concrete, falsework and shores that hold it up until it can carry itself, back-propping that spreads load through floors below, working platforms, scaffolds, hoardings, temporary bracing for steel or precast frames, and crane bases. They are real structures, often carrying loads as large as the permanent ones, but they are designed and built faster, by different people, and with less scrutiny. That is why they fail more often.

The ownership gap

The permanent works engineer designs the finished building and typically disclaims temporary works as the contractor's means and methods. The contractor owns his methods, but may subcontract the formwork to one firm, the scaffold to another and the propping design to a third. Unless the contract assigns overall responsibility, nobody owns the whole picture: each party sees its own piece, and the interfaces, such as the slab that the props stand on, belong to no one.

British practice, after a run of falsework collapses in the early 1970s, developed the idea of a single named temporary works coordinator with authority to stop work, and that idea is widely used elsewhere. In the United States, the equivalent is usually set by the contract and the contractor's own safety programme rather than by a single statute, so the owner should require it expressly.

The lifecycle

A temporary structure goes through a sequence: a design brief stating loads, sequence and constraints; a design by a competent designer; an independent check whose depth matches the risk; erection and inspection against the design; a written permission to load; use and monitoring; and a written permission to strike, or dismantle. The two permissions are where failures are prevented or caused. Most incidents involve a structure loaded before it was ready, or removed before the permanent works could carry the load.

The governing documents

In American practice the key references are ASCE 37 for design loads on structures during construction, ACI 347 for formwork, OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart Q for concrete and masonry construction and Subpart P for excavations, and IBC Chapter 33 for safeguards during construction, with temporary structures addressed in IBC Chapter 31 [unverified — confirm independently]. Verify every document against the current adopted edition; local law governs elsewhere.

A worked example

Consider formwork for a hypothetical concrete wall 3 metres high, cast in one lift.

  1. Fresh concrete behaves like a heavy liquid before it sets. At about 24 kilonewtons per cubic metre, the full liquid pressure at the base of a 3-metre wall is 24 times 3, which is 72 kilopascals.
  2. ACI 347 gives methods to reduce the design pressure where the concrete is placed slowly enough to begin stiffening, depending on placement rate, temperature and mix [unverified — confirm independently]. The full liquid head is the upper bound.
  3. If the formwork was designed for a reduced pressure assuming a slow pour, but the crew pours the wall in twenty minutes from a pump, the actual pressure approaches 72 kilopascals. The design assumption was the placement rate, and nobody told the pump operator.
  4. So a temporary works design is only valid within its stated assumptions: pour rate, temperature, admixtures, sequence. Those assumptions belong on the drawing and on the pour card.

Back-propping on a flat plate

On a flat-plate concrete frame, each new floor is cast on formwork supported by props that stand on the floor below, which is itself young concrete. That floor cannot carry the weight alone, so props continue down through several floors, sharing the load. Back-propping is therefore a calculation, not a habit, and the number of floors propped and the age at which props are removed depend on strength gain and loads. Every commercial incentive points towards striking early, because formwork and props are expensive and the next floor is waiting.

Scaling the check to the risk

Not every temporary structure needs the same scrutiny. A common approach, from British practice, grades the independent check by risk: a simple, standard solution may be checked by another competent person in the same team; a bespoke design by someone independent of the designer; and a complex or high-consequence structure, such as falsework for a transfer slab or excavation support beside a neighbour, by a separate organisation. The owner should ask which category each item on the register falls into and who checked it. A check by the designer's own colleague, sitting at the next desk, is not independent for a structure whose failure would kill.

Also ask what happens when the design changes. A propping layout altered on site to fit around a service riser is a new design, and it needs the same designer and the same check as the original, before it is loaded.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an incentive running unchecked: the crew is paid for speed, the formwork is hired by the week, and striking early is always cheaper today. Only proof, in the form of test results and a signed permission, pushes back.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner accepts "the superintendent handles it" as the answer to who coordinates temporary works. A superintendent has a hundred other priorities. The coordinator must be named, competent, and given the authority to stop work, and his role should be in the contract.

How you will use it

Require a named temporary works coordinator with stop-work authority. Require a temporary works register listing every temporary structure, its designer, its checker and its status. Require the design brief, design, independent check and written permissions to load and strike. Ask to see the back-propping scheme on a concrete frame. Professional sign-off required: a temporary works designer and an independent checking engineer.
checklist: Require a named temporary works coordinator with authority to stop work.
Require a temporary works register: each structure, designer, checker and status.
Require a design brief stating loads, sequence and assumptions for each temporary structure.
Require an independent check scaled to the risk.
Require written permission to load and written permission to strike.
Ask to see the back-propping scheme for every concrete frame.
Make sure design assumptions such as pour rate appear on the pour card.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: You ask who coordinates temporary works and are told, 'The superintendent handles it, and each subcontractor designs its own.' What is wrong, and what do you require?
selftest.a: Nobody owns the whole picture, so the interfaces, such as the slab that props stand on, belong to no one, and the superintendent lacks the time and often the authority to stop work. Require a named, competent temporary works coordinator with stop-work authority, a register of every temporary structure, independent checks, and written permissions to load and strike.

apply: List every temporary structure you would expect on a concrete-framed building from excavation to roof, and note who would design each one.
sources: ASCE 37, ACI 347, OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subparts P and Q, and IBC Chapters 31 and 33 as commonly cited; verify against current editions [unverified — confirm independently]. The temporary works coordinator concept comes from British practice following the 1970s falsework inquiries. Example hypothetical.

title: When the Temporary Holds the Permanent, and Lets Go
summary: Temporary works failures fall into three families: young concrete loaded too soon, temporary structures that fail, and loading sequences nobody checked. Skyline Plaza, Willow Island and L'Ambiance Plaza show the pattern, and the common thread is organisational.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the worst failures during construction happen in the gap between when a structure looks finished and when it is actually strong enough. Every incentive on site points towards closing that gap early, and only proof and written permission push back.

In plain English

Concrete gains strength over days and weeks, more slowly in cold weather. Temporary structures hold it until it is strong enough. If the props come out too early, or new loads go on too soon, the young concrete may fail, and on a multi-storey frame one failing floor can drop onto the next. The physics is well understood. What fails is usually the decision to proceed.

The three families

First, young concrete loaded before it is strong enough, often in cold weather when strength gain is slow and the calendar is the only measure being used. Second, temporary structures themselves failing: shores, falsework, scaffolds or jacks that are overloaded, poorly founded, wrongly assembled or not as designed. Third, loading sequences nobody checked, where each step was reasonable alone but the combination, such as storing materials on a freshly cast floor while props were being moved, exceeded what the structure could take.

The cases

Skyline Plaza, Fairfax County, Virginia, 2 March 1973. A high-rise under construction partly collapsed and 14 workers died. As the public investigation described it, shores were removed from a floor cast in cold weather before the concrete had gained enough strength, the slab failed in punching shear around columns, and the failure progressed downward through the building.

Willow Island, West Virginia, 27 April 1978. During construction of a cooling tower at a power station, a climbing scaffold anchored to the shell fell and 51 workers died. As reported, it was anchored into concrete placed the day before, which had not gained enough strength to hold it.

L'Ambiance Plaza, Bridgeport, Connecticut, 23 April 1987. A lift-slab building, in which floor slabs are cast on the ground and jacked up the columns, collapsed during construction and 28 workers died. It failed in its temporary condition; the precise cause was disputed between investigators.

The early-1970s falsework collapses in Britain led to an inquiry and to the practice of a single named temporary works coordinator with authority to stop work.

These cases are summarised from public investigations and published accounts. Read the primary reports before quoting details.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical slab designed with 30 megapascal concrete, and the temporary works engineer requires 20 megapascals in field-cured cylinders before the props beneath it may be removed.

  1. In mild weather, many mixes reach roughly two thirds of their design strength in about a week, so about 20 megapascals, and "seven days" becomes the habit.
  2. In a cold week, strength gain slows sharply. The same slab at seven days might reach only 12 to 14 megapascals.
  3. The crew strikes at seven days because that is what has always worked. The slab is carrying load at perhaps 60 percent of the strength the engineer required.
  4. Punching shear capacity rises roughly with the square root of concrete strength, so at 13 rather than 20 megapascals the capacity is about 0.8 times what was assumed. On a slab whose margin was small, that is the Skyline Plaza pattern.
  5. The control is simple: field-cured cylinders, or another agreed strength method, tested before striking, and a written permission to strike that cites the result. The calendar is not evidence.

The organisational thread

In each family, someone usually knew enough to stop. The pressure to proceed came from schedule and cost, and the person with the information lacked either the authority or the evidence to say no. That is incentives and agency risk: the people bearing the cost of delay are not the people bearing the risk of collapse. Inversion helps: ask what would have to be true for this structure to fail today, then check each item.

Why progressive collapse matters

Two of these cases spread far beyond the first failure. When one floor of a frame under construction drops, it lands on the floor below with an impact load that floor was never designed for, and the failure can run down the building, one level after another. A finished building has continuity, ties and redundancy that resist this; a building under construction often does not yet, because ties are incomplete and the floors are young. That is why the consequence of a temporary works error on a multi-storey frame is so much larger than the error itself, and why the checks deserve more weight than their cost suggests.

It is also why the people at greatest risk are the crews on the lower floors, finishing work beneath a floor that has just been struck. A safe striking decision protects them as much as the floor itself.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a calendar rule, such as seven days, used in conditions it was never meant for. Cold weather, a different mix or a faster floor cycle all change the answer, and the habit does not notice.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner judges temporary works by looking at them. Props that look straight and tight tell you nothing about the strength of the slab they hold or the floor they stand on. The question is never whether it looks right; it is who signed the permission and what evidence was attached.

How you will use it

Require written permission to strike, citing strength test results, for every suspended concrete element. Ask what the cold-weather procedure is before winter, not during it. Ask how loading sequences on new floors, such as stored materials, are controlled. Make reporting a concern safe and expected. Professional sign-off required: temporary works designer and structural engineer of record.
checklist: Require written permission to strike that cites strength test results.
Ask for the cold-weather concreting procedure before winter arrives.
Never accept a calendar rule as evidence of concrete strength.
Ask how storage and construction loads on young floors are controlled.
Check that temporary structures are founded on something designed to carry them.
Make it safe and expected to report a concern about temporary works.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: In a cold week, the formwork foreman says, 'Seven days has always been fine; we strike tomorrow.' There are no strength results. What do you do?
selftest.a: Ask for the written permission to strike and the strength results it relies on. In cold weather strength gain slows, so seven days may leave the slab well short of the strength the engineer required, which is the Skyline Plaza pattern. Without test evidence and a signed permission, the props stay. Under Design-Build, ask the contractor to confirm compliance in writing rather than instructing the crew yourself.

apply: Write the three items a permission-to-strike form should contain: the element, the required strength with its source, and the test result with date and signature.
sources: Skyline Plaza (1973), Willow Island (1978) and L'Ambiance Plaza (1987) summarised from public investigation reports and published accounts, including work by the US National Bureau of Standards; read the primary reports before quoting details. The square-root relationship for punching shear follows ACI 318 practice as commonly quoted [unverified — confirm independently]. Example hypothetical.

title: Back-Propping Arithmetic: How Many Floors, How Far Apart, and When to Strike
summary: A freshly cast floor puts its weight, its formwork and construction loads into the propping system, which young floors below must share. The arithmetic shows how thin the margin is, why removing one level of props can fail a scheme, and why prop load rises with the square of spacing.
body:
Mr Shabazz, back-propping is a load-sharing calculation on floors that are not yet at full strength, and its margin is often thin. Remove one level too early, or space the props a little wider, and a passing scheme fails.

In plain English

When a new floor is poured on a flat-plate frame, the wet concrete, the formwork and the construction loads are carried by props down to the floor below. That floor, perhaps a week old, cannot carry it all, so the props continue down through two or three floors, and each connected floor takes a share. The scheme specifies how many floors stay propped, how far apart the props are, and when each level may be removed. All numbers here are illustrative.

The load from a fresh floor

Take a hypothetical flat plate 250 millimetres thick.

  1. Wet concrete: 0.25 metres times about 24 kilonewtons per cubic metre is 6.0 kilonewtons per square metre.
  2. Formwork: about 0.5 kilonewtons per square metre.
  3. Construction live load for workers and equipment: a commonly quoted minimum of about 2.4 kilonewtons per square metre, which is 50 pounds per square foot, in ACI 347 practice, with ASCE 37 governing construction loads [unverified — confirm independently].
  4. Total: about 8.9 kilonewtons per square metre into the propping system.

A worked example

Now share that load across the floors below. Suppose each supporting floor, when mature, can carry about 3.6 kilonewtons per square metre of extra load above its own weight before reaching its design limit in punching shear. That is a hypothetical figure from the engineer.

  1. At seven days, assume the concrete has reached about 70 percent of design strength. Punching shear capacity varies roughly with the square root of strength, and the square root of 0.7 is about 0.84, so each young floor can take about 3.6 times 0.84, which is about 3.0 kilonewtons per square metre.
  2. With three connected floors sharing equally, each takes 8.9 divided by 3, about 2.97 kilonewtons per square metre. Against a capacity of about 3.0, it passes, by about one percent. That is a thin margin.
  3. Remove one level of back-props early, leaving two floors to share: 8.9 divided by 2 is 4.45 each. Against 3.0, that is about 48 percent over capacity. It fails.
  4. Equal sharing is itself a simplification; stiffer, older floors attract more load. The real scheme is the engineer's calculation, not this arithmetic.

Prop spacing

Each prop carries the load from the area around it, so prop load rises with the square of the spacing.

  1. On a 1.5 metre grid, each prop carries 1.5 times 1.5, which is 2.25 square metres: 2.25 times 8.9 is about 20 kilonewtons.
  2. On a 1.8 metre grid, 3.24 square metres: about 28.8 kilonewtons. A 20 percent wider spacing means about 44 percent more load per prop.
  3. Prop capacity also falls as the prop is extended, because a longer prop buckles more easily. Read the manufacturer's load table at the actual extended height, not the maximum shown on the brochure.

The floor cycle connection

A faster floor cycle means the supporting floors are younger and weaker when the next floor is cast. If the programme moves from a ten-day cycle to a seven-day cycle, the scheme must be redone, because every floor in the stack is weaker than the design assumed. A schedule acceleration is a structural change to the temporary works.

Margin of safety

A thin margin on uncertain inputs is not really a margin. Strength gain depends on weather and mix, construction loads depend on what the crew stacks on the deck, and load sharing depends on stiffness. When a scheme passes by one percent on estimates, it needs real evidence, such as strength tests and controlled loading, to stay on the right side.

What you can ask without doing the calculation

The owner does not need to run the scheme, but he can ask four questions that expose a weak one. What strength must each floor reach before its props are removed, and how is it measured? How many floors are connected, and what happens to the shares if one level is removed for a delivery? What floor cycle does the scheme assume, and is that the cycle the programme now shows? And who signs each removal? If any answer is "we always do it this way", the scheme is a habit rather than a calculation, and that is the moment to ask for the designer's sheet.

Ask too what happens at the edges. Props near a slab edge, a stair opening or a lift core carry more than the average share, and the scheme should show them, rather than a uniform grid drawn across the whole floor as though every bay were the same.

Finally, ask how the props are founded on the lowest level. A back-propping stack that ends on a ground slab or on compacted fill depends on that base not settling under concentrated load, which is a separate check from the slabs above.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is quietly removing one level of back-props to free equipment for the next floor. On paper it is a small change; in the arithmetic it can turn a pass into a failure by nearly half.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads a prop's capacity from the brochure headline. Capacity depends on extension, and a prop at full extension may carry far less than its rated maximum.

How you will use it

Ask to see the back-propping scheme, the number of floors propped, the prop grid, the strength required before each removal, and the floor cycle it assumes. If the programme accelerates, ask for the scheme to be rechecked. Ask how stored materials on new floors are limited. Professional sign-off required: temporary works designer, with the structural engineer of record confirming the slab capacities used.
checklist: Ask for the back-propping scheme with floors propped, grid and removal criteria.
Check the floor cycle the scheme assumes against the programme.
Require a recheck whenever the floor cycle is accelerated.
Never allow a level of back-props to be removed without written permission.
Read prop capacity at the actual extended height from the manufacturer's table.
Ask how stored materials on young floors are limited.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: To free props for the next floor, the contractor proposes keeping only two floors back-propped instead of three. Using a fresh-floor load of 8.9 kilonewtons per square metre and a young-floor capacity of 3.0, what does that do?
selftest.a: With three floors each carries about 2.97, just under 3.0. With two floors each carries about 4.45, roughly 48 percent over capacity. The proposal turns a thin pass into a clear fail. It needs the temporary works designer's recalculation and written approval, which on these numbers it would not get.

apply: Compute prop loads for the 8.9 kilonewton per square metre floor at grids of 1.2, 1.5 and 1.8 metres, and note the percentage change.
sources: Construction loads as commonly quoted from ACI 347 and ASCE 37; the square-root relationship for punching shear capacity follows ACI 318 practice [unverified — confirm independently]. Slab capacities and strength gain are hypothetical; the real scheme is the engineer's calculation. All figures illustrative.

title: Hold Points: The Inspection and Test Plan That Makes the Calculation Govern
summary: A calculation governs nothing on site until hold points make it govern. An inspection and test plan lists every check, its criterion, who does it and whether work must stop for it, and the nonconformance register shows whether anyone is actually recording.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a temporary works design only protects the building if somebody checks the work against it before the next step starts. Hold points are how that happens, and a signed release is the evidence that it did.

In plain English

An inspection and test plan, an ITP, is a table for each type of work listing the steps, what is checked at each step, against which document, by whom, the acceptance criterion, the record produced, and the level of inspection. It turns the drawings and specification into a sequence of checks the site actually performs.

Three levels of inspection

Review means records are checked afterwards; work proceeds. Witness means notice is given so a named person can attend; if nobody attends, work may proceed. Hold means work stops until a named person has inspected and released it in writing. Hold points are expensive in waiting time, so they belong only where the step is irreversible or the consequence of error is severe.

An ITP for one floor of a flat plate

For each floor, a reasonable plan might include:

  1. Formwork and propping erected to design: permit to load signed by the temporary works coordinator. Hold.
  2. Back-props below confirmed in place to the scheme. Hold.
  3. Reinforcement checked and released, with punching shear reinforcement at columns on its own line, because it is the most consequential and the easiest to omit. Hold.
  4. Pour card signed by every trade with embedded items: electrical, plumbing, mechanical sleeves, fire stopping. Hold.
  5. Fresh concrete sampled and cylinders made under ASTM C31 and tested under ASTM C39 [unverified — confirm independently]. Witness.
  6. Permit to strike formwork, citing strength results. Hold.
  7. Back-prop removal, level by level, to the scheme. Hold.

Six of those seven are hold points, because each covers an irreversible step or one where an error is structural.

A worked example

Suppose a hold point on reinforcement costs a crew of 8 a two-hour wait while the inspector arrives, at a hypothetical 60 per hour each.

  1. Cost of the wait: 8 times 2 times 60, which is 960 per floor.
  2. Across ten floors, about 9,600.
  3. The inspector finds punching shear reinforcement missing at two columns on one floor. Fixing it before the pour takes half a day.
  4. Discovering it after the pour means investigation, possibly coring, a retrofit designed by the engineer and installed from below, and perhaps weeks of delay at the combined weekly cost of time. At 60,000 a week, two weeks is 120,000 before any repair.
  5. The hold point paid for itself many times on one floor. Its value is not average; it is in the one time it catches something.

The nonconformance register

A nonconformance report, NCR, records work that does not meet the requirement and how it was resolved. On any real project, some work fails some check. A register showing zero entries after months of work does not mean perfect quality; it usually means nobody is recording. Treat an empty register as an honesty test the project has failed.

Certification is not performance

A contractor's ISO 9001 certification shows that a quality management system exists and has been audited. It does not show that the system is working on your site this week. Sample the records yourself.

The owner's role under Design-Build

Require the inspection and test plan as a contract deliverable before work starts, require it to be followed, and sample it: pick a floor or an element and ask to see every signed release for it. Never sign the releases yourself and never direct how a nonconformance is fixed, because both move responsibility back onto the owner.

Who releases what

Each hold point names the person who may release it, and that name matters. The temporary works coordinator releases a permit to load; the engineer of record or his delegate, and the special inspector where the code requires one, release reinforcement; each trade foreman signs his own embedded items on the pour card; and the temporary works designer's criteria, checked by the coordinator, release striking. A release signed by the person whose crew is waiting is not independent. Ask for a short matrix showing each hold point and who is authorised to release it, and check a sample of signatures against it.

Keep the records retrievable. Releases filed by floor and element, with photographs taken immediately before concrete arrives, let anyone answer later what was checked, when and by whom. That record is also what a lender's monitor, an insurer or a future buyer will ask for when they need evidence that hidden work was done properly.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a release signed after the event: a pour card dated the morning after the pour, a permit to strike completed retrospectively. The paperwork exists and the check did not happen.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner looks at the plan and not at the records. A well-written ITP that nobody follows is worse than a short one that is followed, because it gives false comfort. Check dates and times against the site diary and the concrete delivery tickets.

How you will use it

Require the ITP before work starts, with hold points at irreversible steps. Ask for the NCR register at every meeting and be concerned if it is empty. Sample releases on an element you choose, checking dates and times. Professional sign-off required: the contractor's quality manager, the temporary works coordinator, and the special inspector for code-required inspections.
checklist: Require an inspection and test plan before each type of work starts.
Put hold points at irreversible or high-consequence steps.
Give punching shear reinforcement its own line in the reinforcement release.
Require a pour card signed by every trade with embedded items.
Ask for the nonconformance register at every meeting; treat an empty one as a warning.
Sample releases on an element you choose and check dates against delivery tickets.
Never sign releases or direct fixes yourself under Design-Build.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Sampling records for one floor, you find the pour card signed and dated the day after the concrete delivery tickets, and the NCR register has no entries in four months. What do these tell you?
selftest.a: The pour card was completed after the event, so the pre-pour check probably did not happen as a hold point, and an empty NCR register after four months suggests nobody is recording problems. Raise both in writing, ask for an explanation and corrective action from the contractor's quality manager, and increase your sampling. Do not direct the fix yourself.

apply: Draft a five-line inspection and test plan for one hypothetical activity, giving the check, document, responsible person, criterion and inspection level for each line.
sources: Inspection and test plans, hold and witness points and NCR registers follow common quality management practice; ISO 9001 is a management system standard. ASTM C31 and C39 as commonly cited for concrete cylinders [unverified — confirm independently]. Example hypothetical.

title: Week Six Review: Who Signed the Permit, and What Evidence Was Attached
summary: Six scenario questions on temporary works ownership, failure patterns, back-propping arithmetic and hold points. The week's thread is that on temporary works the question is never whether it looks right, but who released it and on what evidence.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week dealt with structures that disappear when the building is finished and cause a disproportionate share of its worst accidents. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

Question 1. You ask who coordinates temporary works on your frame and the answer is, "The superintendent handles it." Why is that not good enough?

Answer. Because temporary works sit in the gap between the permanent engineer, who disclaims them, and several subcontractors, each designing his own piece. The interfaces, such as the floors props stand on, belong to nobody unless someone is named to own the whole. Require a named, competent temporary works coordinator with authority to stop work, a register of every temporary structure, independent checks, and written permissions to load and strike.

Question 2. A wall form designed for a slow placement is about to be filled in twenty minutes by pump. Why does it matter?

Answer. Fresh concrete acts like a heavy liquid until it begins to stiffen, so a rapid pour approaches full liquid pressure: about 24 kilopascals per metre of height, 72 at the base of a 3-metre wall. A design that assumed a slow placement rate assumed a lower pressure. The pour rate is a design assumption and belongs on the pour card.

Question 3. In a cold week, a crew plans to strike props at seven days "as always", with no strength results. What pattern is this, and what do you require?

Answer. It is the Skyline Plaza pattern: young concrete in cold weather carrying load before it is strong enough, failing in punching shear and progressing downward. Require field-cured strength results that meet the engineer's stated striking strength, and a written permission to strike citing them. The calendar is not evidence.

Question 4. A fresh floor puts 8.9 kilonewtons per square metre into the propping. Each young floor can take about 3.0. What happens with three floors sharing, and with two?

Answer. Three floors carry about 2.97 each, a pass by about one percent. Two floors carry 4.45 each, about 48 percent over. Removing one level of back-props turns a thin pass into a clear failure. Any change needs the designer's recalculation and written approval.

Question 5. The props are moved from a 1.5 metre grid to a 1.8 metre grid to speed up stripping. What happens to the load per prop?

Answer. Load per prop goes with the area each carries, the square of the spacing: from 2.25 to 3.24 square metres, about 44 percent more load per prop. At the same time capacity falls with extension. Read the manufacturer's table at the actual height and get the change approved in writing.

Question 6. Sampling one floor, you find releases dated after the pour and an NCR register with no entries in five months. What do you conclude, and what do you do?

Answer. The hold points are not working as hold points; the paperwork is being completed after the work, and nobody is recording nonconformances. Raise it in writing with the contractor's quality manager, ask for corrective action, and increase your sampling. Under Design-Build, require and sample the system; do not sign releases or direct fixes.

Recap

Temporary works are real structures carrying large, uncertain loads, built faster and with less scrutiny than permanent works, which is why they fail more often. They fall between the permanent engineer and the contractor's methods, so the owner requires a named coordinator with stop-work authority. Their lifecycle runs through brief, design, independent check, erection and inspection, permission to load, use, and permission to strike. The two permissions are where failures are prevented.

The failure families are young concrete loaded too soon, temporary structures that fail, and loading sequences nobody checked. Skyline Plaza, Willow Island and L'Ambiance Plaza show the human pattern: someone knew enough to stop, and the pressure to proceed won.

Back-propping is a load-sharing calculation on weak young floors, often with a thin margin. Removing a level of props or widening the grid can fail a scheme, and a faster floor cycle changes every number.

Hold points make the calculation govern. An inspection and test plan lists each check and its level; a signed release is the evidence; an empty nonconformance register is a warning; and certification is not performance.

The thread: on temporary works the question is never whether it looks right. It is who signed the permission, and what evidence was attached. Professional sign-off required: temporary works designer, independent checking engineer, structural engineer of record, and the contractor's quality manager.

One question carries across every lesson this week and into the next: what is the evidence? Strength is evidenced by test results, not days; a safe propping scheme by a signed calculation, not experience; a completed check by a dated release, not a verbal assurance. When the evidence is missing, the owner's job is not to supply an answer but to ask for the missing record, in writing, from the person responsible for producing it.

Next week goes back into the ground, this time permanently: how shallow ground carries a building, the two separate tests every foundation must pass, and why on soft ground it is the second test that decides.
checklist: Name a temporary works coordinator with stop-work authority.
Treat pour rate and striking strength as design assumptions on the pour card.
Refuse calendar-based striking without strength evidence.
Recheck back-propping whenever levels, grid or floor cycle change.
Sample hold-point releases and check their dates.
Treat an empty nonconformance register as a warning.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: What two documents would you ask for first to judge whether a concrete frame's temporary works are under control?
selftest.a: The temporary works register, showing every temporary structure with its designer, checker and status, and a sample of signed permissions to load and strike for a floor you choose, with the strength results they cite and dates that precede the work.

apply: From memory, write the seven lifecycle stages of a temporary structure and the three levels of inspection, then check them against this week's lessons.
